report:
**Conclusion: Likely true, with moderate-to-strong evidence — higher olive oil intake, especially replacing butter/margarine, is associated with lower stroke risk, though effect size varies by study design.**

The strongest causal evidence comes from the PREDIMED randomized controlled trial in Spain, which found that a Mediterranean diet supplemented with extra-virgin olive oil (~4 tbsp/day) significantly reduced incidence of stroke, myocardial infarction, and cardiovascular death compared to a control lower-fat diet (ahajournals.org, sciencedirect.com/PREDIMED cardiovascular outcomes paper). This is a large, high-quality randomized trial (n>7,000), giving it strong causal weight, though participants were already at high cardiovascular risk, limiting generalizability to the general population.

Large prospective cohort studies support this: a pooled meta-analysis (~101,460 participants) found roughly a 26% lower stroke risk with about two tablespoons of olive oil daily (myolivea.com), and observational analyses from the Nurses' Health Study/Health Professionals Follow-Up Study and other cohorts link higher olive oil consumption with lower cardiovascular disease and stroke risk (webmd.com citing Clin Nutr 2022 study). The Three-City Study also found associations between olive oil consumption/plasma oleic acid and reduced stroke incidence.

Caveats: cohort studies show association, not proof of causation, and benefits may partly reflect broader Mediterranean dietary patterns (more vegetables, fruit, whole grains) rather than olive oil alone. Effect sizes differ by study (19–40% relative risk reduction), and benefits appear strongest for extra-virgin olive oil specifically, and when it replaces less healthy fats like butter or margarine.

**Overall**: Evidence from both an RCT and multiple large cohorts supports the claim that higher olive oil consumption is associated with reduced stroke risk, particularly extra-virgin olive oil replacing saturated fats.
